newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea faces 300,000T a year rice deficit - embassy.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea faces 300,000T a year rice deficit - embassy.

text.p: South Korea will face chronic annual rice deficits of up to 300,000 tonnes a year within five years and this will force it to become a significant annual importer of table rice, a U.S. embassy report said on Friday.

South Korea's agriculture ministry has projected rice consumption will once again exceed domestic production in the 1997 marketing year (November 1996/October 1997), leading to a further decline in stocks, the report said.
Assuming average harvests, the trend in declining stock levels will continue through the foreseeable future.
Rice consumption is once again expected to outstrip production, resuming a trend interrupted by last year's bumper harvest, the report said.

The ministry estimates end-October rice stocks this year will total 605,000 tonnes. This translates into 12 percent of annual consumption or approximately six weeks supply -- significantly below the FAO's recommended level, it said.
The buildup reflected last year's bumper crop, with production exceeding anticipated annual consumption by 280,000 tonnes, it said.
Though the ministry was reluctant to provide official data, there was reportedly slightly less than 100,000 tonnes of imported rice still held in stocks, it said.

Of the 51,000 tonnes of Indian rice, approximately 17,000 tonnes has been processed by manufacturers of "makkoli", a traditional fermented rice wine. All of the remaining rice -- including the Indian long graing and the Chinese medium grain -- remained in storage, it said.
Last year's bumper crop ended three consecutive years of disappointing harvest that has left South Korea with sharply reduced stocks, it said.
According to revised statistics by the ministry, South Korea's rice stock had fallen to 217,000 tonnes at the end of October 1996, the report said.
This represented less than five percent of annual consumption, or approximately a 15-day supply, well belowed the targeted level of 17 percent of annual consumption as recommended by FAO, it said.
Anecdotal reports at the time indicated that the warehouses and rice mills were vertually empty during the pre-harvest period in early last October, it said.
Apparently the country's entire rice supply was limited to the milled rice already in the wholesale or retail distribution chain, it said.
A damaging typhoon during the month of September and October -- not all that uncommon on the Korean peninsula -- could have proved disastrous for the government, it said.
The fact that the government would allow rice stocks to deteriorate to such a dangerously low level is an indication on just how politically sensitive the rice issue is in South Korea, it said.
It is also a good indication on just how determined the current administration is to limit imports to the annual MMA levels, it said.
It should be noted that the ministry recently published a correction in the ending stock levels, which resulted in the revised ending stock figures noted above, it said.

The ministry adjusted the ending stock level for October 1994 to 680,000 tonnes from the previous figure of 822,000 tonnes with a concomitant increase in the marketing year 1994 loss figure to 349,000 tonnes from 198,000 tonnes. No explanation was given for the adjustment, it said.
